questions.text: What is the value of √0.0049 × √1.44?
How many zeros are there at the end of 125! (125 factorial)?
How many three-digit numbers are divisible by 7?
questions.explanation: The first is 105 and the last is 994. Count = (994 − 105)/7 + 1 = 127 + 1 = 128.

questions.text: Nisha's salary is first increased by 20%, then decreased by 20%, and then increased by 10%. What is the net change in her salary?
questions.explanation: Net factor = 1.2 × 0.8 × 1.1 = 1.056, which is a 5.6% increase.

questions.text: A dishonest grocer sells rice at cost price but uses a 900 g weight in place of a 1 kg weight. What is his gain percentage?
questions.explanation: He gives 900 g but charges for 1000 g. Gain = 100/900 × 100 = 11.11%.

questions.text: A sum of money doubles itself in 5 years at compound interest. In how many years will it become 8 times itself at the same rate?
questions.explanation: 8 = 2³, so it must double three times: 3 × 5 = 15 years.

questions.text: Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 7. If 6 is added to each, the ratio becomes 3 : 4. What is the larger number?
A batter's average after a certain number of innings is 32. After scoring 98 in the next innings, the average rises to 35. How many innings has the batter played in total now?
questions.explanation: If n innings were played before, 32n + 98 = 35(n + 1), so 3n = 63 and n = 21. Including the latest innings, the total is 22.

questions.text:
Statements:
All cups are plates.
All plates are bowls.

Conclusions:
I. All cups are bowls.
II. Some bowls are cups.

Assuming the statements are true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, which conclusion(s) logically follow?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
questions.explanation: All cups are plates and all plates are bowls, so all cups are bowls (I). Since cups exist and are all bowls, some bowls are cups (II).

questions.text: Find the next term in the series: C3, F9, I27, L81, ?
questions.explanation: Letters move 3 places forward (C, F, I, L, O) and numbers are multiplied by 3 (3, 9, 27, 81, 243).

questions.text: Six students — R, S, T, U, V and W — scored different marks in a test. R scored more than S but less than T. U scored less than S. V scored more than T. W scored less than R but more than U. Who scored the third highest marks?
questions.explanation: V > T > R, and everyone else (S, W, U) is below R. So R is third, whatever the order of S and W.

questions.text: Which is the next year after 2026 that will have exactly the same calendar as 2026?
questions.explanation: 2026 is not a leap year and starts on a Thursday. Adding odd days (1 for a normal year, 2 for a leap year) from 2026 reaches a multiple of 7 at 2037, which is also a non-leap year.

questions.text: Find the wrong number in the series: 2, 5, 14, 41, 123, 365
questions.explanation: Each term is three times the previous term minus 1: 2, 5, 14, 41, 122, 365. So 123 should be 122.

questions.text: A family has six members — A, B, C, D, E and F — with two married couples. D is the grandmother of A and the mother of B. C is the wife of B and the mother of F. F is the only granddaughter of E. How is A related to F?
questions.explanation: The two couples must be D–E and B–C, so A and F are the children of B and C. F is E's only granddaughter, so A is a grandson. A is F's brother.

questions.text:
Statements: A ≥ B > C;  C < D ≤ E;  F > A

Conclusions:
I. B > D
II. F > E

Which of the conclusions is definitely true?
options: Both I and II are definitely true
Neither I nor II is definitely true
questions.explanation: B and D are both greater than C, but they cannot be compared with each other. F > A ≥ B > C and E ≥ D > C give no link between F and E. So neither conclusion is definitely true.

questions.text:
Each question below has two statements. Decide whether the data in the statements is sufficient to answer the question.

Question: What is the value of x + y?
I. 2x + 3y = 12
II. 4x + 6y = 24
options: Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not
Both statements together are not sufficient
questions.explanation: Statement II is just statement I multiplied by 2, so together they are one equation in two unknowns. Different pairs (for example x = 6, y = 0 and x = 0, y = 4) give different values of x + y.

questions.text:
Choose the word or phrase closest in meaning to 'candid' as used in the sentence.

The new manager was candid about the challenges the team would face.
questions.explanation: 'Candid' means open and honest, i.e. frank.

questions.text:
Rearrange the sentences P, Q, R and S to form a coherent paragraph. Choose the correct order.

P. Rather than wait for the municipality to act, she set up a small library in the community hall.
Q. She soon noticed that the children in her colony had few books to read at home.
R. Kavita moved to Bhopal after retiring as a school teacher.
S. Today, more than fifty children borrow books from it every week.
questions.explanation: R introduces Kavita; Q describes the problem she noticed; P gives her response; S ('from it', the library) describes the present result.

questions.text: Which of the following sentences about today's news is grammatically correct?
options: The newses are very encouraging today.
The news is very encouraging today.
The news are very encouraging today.
The news were very encouraging today.
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun that looks plural but takes a singular verb.

questions.text:
What does the phrase 'learnt the ropes' mean in the sentence below?

The new intern quickly learnt the ropes at the office.
questions.explanation: 'To learn the ropes' means to learn how a particular job or activity is done.

questions.text:
The sentence below is divided into four parts. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error.

Each boy and each girl / in the class / have to submit / a project report.
questions.explanation: When subjects joined by 'and' are each preceded by 'each' or 'every', the verb is singular: 'has to submit'.

questions.text:
Choose the correct passive form of the sentence:

They are repairing the bridge.
options: The bridge is repaired by them.
The bridge has been repairing by them.
The bridge is being repaired by them.
The bridge was being repaired by them.
questions.explanation: Present continuous active (are repairing) becomes 'is being' + past participle in the passive.

questions.text:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Some people dismiss board games as old-fashioned in an age of smartphones. This view overlooks what such games offer: face-to-face conversation, patience, and the experience of losing gracefully. Families who set aside one evening a week for a board game often say it is the only time everyone sits together without a screen.

The author's attitude towards board games is best described as:
questions.explanation: The author rejects the view that board games are old-fashioned and lists their benefits, which shows appreciation.

questions.text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.

The new bridge ______ by the time the monsoon begins next June.
questions.explanation: An action that will be finished before a future time takes the future perfect; the bridge is acted upon, so the passive 'will have been completed' is needed.

questions.text:
What will be the output of the following pseudocode?

Integer arr[5] = {5, 7, 5, 3, 7}
Integer x
Set x = 0
for (each i from 0 to 4)
    x = x XOR arr[i]
end for
Print x

(XOR is the bitwise exclusive-OR operator. Array indices start at 0.)
questions.explanation: Equal values cancel under XOR (5 ⊕ 5 = 0, 7 ⊕ 7 = 0), leaving 3.

questions.text:
What will be the output of the following pseudocode?

Integer a, b
Set a = 6, b = 4
for (each i from 1 to 3)
    a = a + b
    b = a - b
end for
Print a + b

What will be the output of the following pseudocode?

Integer fun(Integer x)
    if ((x mod 2) == 0)
        return x / 2
    end if
    return 3 * x + 1
End function

Integer n, steps
Set n = 6, steps = 0
while (n != 1)
    n = fun(n)
    steps = steps + 1
end while
Print steps

What will be the output of the following pseudocode?

Integer count    // global variable
Set count = 0

Integer fun(Integer n)
    count = count + 1
    if (n <= 1)
        return 1
    end if
    return fun(n - 1) + fun(n - 2)
End function

fun(5)
Print count
A wall clock strikes once at 1 o'clock, twice at 2 o'clock, and so on up to 12 times at 12 o'clock. It strikes only on the hour. How many times does it strike in 12 hours?
A grocer wants to weigh any whole number of kilograms from 1 kg to 31 kg on a balance, placing the weights only on one pan. What is the minimum number of weights he needs?
questions.explanation: With weights of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 kg, every value from 1 to 31 is a unique sum (like binary digits). Four weights can make at most 2⁴ − 1 = 15 different non-zero totals, which is not enough for 31.
